title: Vertical, Horizontal and Platform Integration Across Technology Eras

paras: How companies expand, consolidate, compete, decline and reorganize their infrastructure and business models.

Vertical: adjacent stages of a value chain. Horizontal: comparable activities or competitors. Neither guarantees monopoly. Vertical integration combines successive stages of a value chain, such as chip design, device manufacturing, operating system, application distribution and customer service. Horizontal integration combines comparable products, companies or markets at the same stage. Platform integration coordinates independent groups through common interfaces, rules, payments, identity and distribution. These strategies may coexist in one corporation.

blocks.h2: How organizations grow, plateau and decline
paras: A technology market can pass through experimentation, expansion, standardization, consolidation, maturity and partial displacement. These are patterns, not mandatory stages. Product decline can coexist with continued use: mainframes remain important in finance, copper still carries traffic, and Web 1.0-style static documents remain useful. New architectures often absorb old capabilities rather than eliminate them.

Early accounting systems processed records in batches. MRP coordinated manufacturing materials; MRP II expanded manufacturing planning; ERP integrated finance, procurement, inventory and HR. Client-server ERP relied on enterprise databases and LAN/WAN links. SaaS ERP shifted operations and upgrades toward the vendor. API-connected platforms then linked suppliers, payments, logistics and analytics. AI assistants may augment forecasting and user interaction, but transaction integrity and financial controls remain essential.

A firm may initially integrate hardware and software to ensure compatibility, then open APIs to attract partners. Later, rivals may compete at the application layer while infrastructure providers consolidate. Conversely, a platform may integrate vertically into chips, data centers or content to reduce dependency and control performance. Integration is not synonymous with monopoly: relevant market definition, substitutability, entry barriers and regulatory context determine competition outcomes.
